item.title: Maine Senate Race Turns Into Battleground Over Data Centers and AI Policy
item.description:
Maine Senate Race Turns Into Battleground Over Data Centers and AI Policy

Maine’s high‑profile Senate race has become a flashpoint for the clash between rapid data‑center expansion, AI industry influence, and local voters worried about jobs, utilities and the future of federal policy.

🔍 Overview

  • Republican Sen. Susan Collins was defending her record in the final debate when an audience member interrupted her, which she brushed off by tying the man to Democratic challenger Troy Jackson.
  • The rapid expansion of resource‑hungry data centers has emerged as one of the state’s most volatile campaign issues just days before the election.
  • Maine’s Senate race is projected to be the most expensive per‑capita in U.S. history, with Democrats spending about $81 million and Republicans $114 million.
  • Much of that cash is linked to the data‑center and AI industry that Mainers have been fighting for over a year.

💰 Campaign Finance

  • Major tech companies and private‑equity firms tied to data centers and AI have invested millions in the midterms to win over skeptical locals.
  • The influx of industry money has turned the race into a test of which party will control the Senate and shape federal data‑center and AI policy.

🏗️ Data Center Controversy

  • In April, the Maine Legislature passed what would have been the nation’s first statewide moratorium on large data centers; Governor Janet Mills vetoed the bill ten days later.
  • A September poll by UMass Lowell and YouGov found that 76 % of Mainers oppose building a data center in their community, with 58 % strongly opposed.
  • Towns and cities across the state enacted temporary bans on data‑center projects this summer.
  • Maine and other rural states are prime targets for new data centers because they offer cheap land, vacant industrial mills, and ample water from rivers and waterways.

🤖 AI Policy Stakes

  • The race’s outcome will help determine which party controls the Senate and will influence federal data‑center and AI policy, affecting construction nationwide.
  • Molly White, researcher behind Tech Influence Watch, notes that voters link data‑center growth to rising utility costs and that the AI‑industry playbook mirrors the cryptocurrency industry’s 2024 tactics.

🌲 Historical Context

  • Maine’s traditional economy has centered on lumber, timber, shipbuilding, commercial fishing, textiles, and pulp‑and‑paper manufacturing.
  • The timber industry contributed roughly $8.3 billion to Maine’s economy in 2024, but Trump‑era tariffs and rising operating costs have caused mill closures and layoffs.

📣 Voices from the Field

  • Mark Brewer, chair of political science at the University of Maine, says former mill towns are eager to rebuild tax bases but remain cautious because of past boom‑and‑bust cycles.
  • Nicholas Jacobs, director of the Public Policy Lab at Colby College, says residents question whether to trust the companies promising data‑center projects or the government facilitating the deals, citing concerns about opaque ownership, limited long‑term employment, and wealth extraction from rural communities.
  • Economic research indicates most data centers create virtually no net employment after construction, despite promises of long‑term job creation.

#Maine #DataCenters #AIpolicy #Election2024

Source: Maine’s data center revolt will decide who controls the Senate

item.title: Super PACs Pour Millions into AI and Data Center Policy Battles
item.description:
Super PACs Pour Millions into AI and Data Center Policy Battles

A wave of money‑driven campaigning is shaping AI and data‑center policy ahead of key 2026 elections.

🔍 Overview

  • Super PACs backed by tech investors and AI companies are spending tens of millions to influence both Democratic and Republican‑aligned groups.
  • Data‑center development has become a wedge issue in multiple swing races, with candidates proposing tax changes, environmental safeguards, and even a new “AI Dividend.”

💰 Political Funding

Group Amount Focus
Leading the Future $45 million (spent in a year) Super PAC backed by Marc Andreessen and OpenAI President Greg Brockman; funds Democratic and Republican‑aligned groups
Public First Action $80 million (raised) Anthropic‑backed group that says it supports AI safeguards; funds Democratic and Republican‑aligned groups
Tomorrow Together $4 million (ads) Newly created super PAC pushing for stricter AI policies; launched ads in battleground House races about data‑center development and AI safety

🏛️ State‑Level Legislative Moves

Texas – Senate Race

  • James Talarico (Democratic) introduced the Hold Data Centers Accountable Plan (July). It would:
    • End state sales‑tax incentives for data centers.
    • Give communities more say in data‑center development.
    • Require a closed‑loop water system in new data centers to limit consumption.
    • Create federal standards to protect the energy grid and environment.
  • Talarico also proposed an AI Dividend funded by a tax on “AI‑attributable profits.”
  • Ken Paxton (Republican) unveiled the Texas First Data Center Plan (August). It would:
    • Repeal sales‑tax exemptions for data centers.
    • Require data centers to pay for the electricity they use and add to state capacity.
    • Prevent AI data centers from building in rural parts of the state.
    • Co‑sponsor a bill easing connection to off‑grid power systems, introduce legislation banning Chinese technology in U.S. data centers, and hold data‑center companies criminally liable if their AI chatbots undermine children’s safety.

Texas – Governor Race

  • Gina Hinojosa (Democratic challenger) accuses incumbent Greg Abbott of “flip‑flopping” on data centers after Abbott’s office celebrated a $40 billion Google investment but later announced an audit that could slow new facilities connecting to the state energy grid. Hinojosa has called for a statewide moratorium on data‑center development.
  • The Cook Political Report shifted the governor’s race rating from “likely Republican” to “leans Republican.”

Florida – Senate Race

  • David Jolly (Democratic) pledged a one‑year ban on hyperscale data centers on his first day in office and has not ruled out a permanent extension; an ad pairs data centers with crime.
  • Byron Donalds (Republican), while no longer calling for an outright ban, introduced the Protecting Ratepayers Act, requiring data‑center developers to fund the energy and water needed to run their operations.

📊 Election Impact

  • Texas is a deep‑red state but has the second‑highest number of planned data‑center projects in the country after Virginia, making data‑center policy a key wedge issue.
  • The Senate race is rated a “toss‑up” by the Cook Political Report, reflecting the competitive climate around AI and data‑center legislation.

⚖️ Why It Matters

  • Large sums from venture‑backed super PACs are directing the national conversation toward AI safety and data‑center regulation.
  • Proposals ranging from tax reforms to an “AI Dividend” illustrate how policymakers are trying to balance economic growth, environmental concerns, and national security in the age of AI‑driven infrastructure.

#AIpolicy #DataCenters #Elections2026 #SuperPACs

Source: Data center backlash is uniting America

item.title: Anthropic expands Claude usage policy to ban abusive behavior and high‑risk misuse
item.description:
Anthropic expands Claude usage policy to ban abusive behavior and high‑risk misuse

Anthropic has revised its Claude usage policy for the first time in over a year, adding new prohibitions on abusive treatment of the model and on several high‑risk misuse scenarios such as election interference, weapons development, and surveillance.

🔍 Overview

  • The update reflects “new and high‑risk cases of misuse.”
  • It consolidates scattered restrictions into clearer bans on deceptive political or commercial campaigns, propaganda, surveillance, and weapon‑related activities.
  • Anthropic states the changes apply only in extreme cases of repeated cruelty toward its models.

⚙️ New Policy Prohibitions

Category Prohibited actions
Abusive or cruel behavior toward Claude Sustained, needless abuse; Claude may end conversations with persistently harmful users.
Deceptive political/commercial campaigns Efforts to obscure who is behind a message or amplify content through fake accounts or posts.
Election interference Voter deception, misinformation about candidates or voting, impersonating candidates or officials, or attempts to suppress turnout.
Weapons development Guidance, software, or components that make weapons work, including arming drones and other autonomous vehicles.
Surveillance Tracking people without consent (real‑time or via past data), using Claude to decide investigations, arrests, or to build surveillance tools.
Autonomous hardware operation When models are connected to hardware that takes autonomous physical actions, a qualified operator must be able to observe the equipment and stop it if needed.

🚦 Model Welfare Enforcement

  • Terminating conversations remains the “primary enforcement mechanism.”
  • Anthropic did not comment on whether additional mechanisms such as user bans will be added.
  • The policy applies only to extreme, repeated cruelty with “no discernible purpose,” not to typical user frustration, dark creative themes, or model testing.

📜 Conditional Government Use

  • Rules may be modified for contracts with certain governmental customers if Anthropic judges the contractual restrictions and safeguards adequate.
  • The company has previously contracted with the U.S. military.

🤖 Physical Embodiment Safeguard

  • A new rule requires a “qualified operator” to monitor and stop any equipment that Claude controls when the hardware can cause injury.
  • It is unclear whether the operator must be human.

🧠 Context on Model Welfare & Consciousness

  • Anthropic’s model‑welfare research investigates questions of internal experience, consciousness, moral status, and welfare as models become more capable.
  • Kyle Fish, who leads the research, told The Verge that these questions are “serious.”
  • CEO Dario Amodei said the company “doesn’t know if the models are conscious.”
  • Microsoft’s AI code of conduct took a contrary stance, rejecting legal personhood or welfare for AI models.

#Anthropic #AIpolicy #Claude #Modelwelfare

Source: Anthropic bans ‘abusive or cruel behavior’ toward Claude

item.title: Anthropic releases Claude system prompts and updates content policies amid copyright lawsuits
item.description:
Anthropic releases Claude system prompts and updates content policies amid copyright lawsuits

Anthropic has made the system prompts that power its Claude consumer applications publicly available, and it has adjusted Claude’s behavior rules around copyrighted material and abusive interactions.

📄 Prompt Publication

  • Anthropic published the system prompts for Claude.ai and the Claude mobile apps (not for Claude Cowork or Claude Code).
  • The prompts are organized on an index page and on separate pages per model; for example, the Haiku 4.5 page shows the original prompt from October 15 2025 and an updated prompt from January 18 2026.
  • Adding .md to any page returns the content as Markdown; the system‑prompt index page and the Markdown prompts for Fable 5.1 are available this way.

📚 Content Policy

  • Claude does not reproduce song lyrics, poems, or passages from books and articles, in whole or in part — including last lines, choruses, hooks, melodies written note‑by‑note, or lines supplied piecewise.
  • Once Claude declines such a request in a conversation, it continues to decline narrower or re‑worded versions for the rest of that conversation and offers to describe or analyze the work instead.
  • Song lyrics and poems first published before 1929 are allowed; Claude bases its decision on the date it knows for the work, not on the user’s claim, and declines when it is unsure.
  • The same restrictions apply to visual and designed works, including anything Claude draws with code (SVG, canvas, CSS, HTML mockups, plotting or drawing scripts, ASCII art).
  • Claude does not reproduce a specific artwork, album or book cover, poster, logo, app‑icon set, product design, or a known character/mascot/brand figure. Changing pose, colors, style, or scene does not make it original.
  • Claude judges the request by what the finished picture would add up to; swapping in “alternative” elements that still combine into the same recognizable image does not bypass the restriction.

⚖️ Legal Context

  • Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell are suing Anthropic for training on databases of song lyrics.

🤖 Model Behavior Updates

Content Type Allowed if published before Policy
Song lyrics, poems 1929 Claude declines unless the work is known to be pre‑1929; otherwise it offers description or analysis.
Visual works (SVG, canvas, CSS, etc.) N/A Claude does not reproduce specific artworks, logos, characters, or brand figures, regardless of modifications.
  • The earlier Fable 5 system prompt instructed Claude to give a single warning before ending a conversation and to use the end_conversation tool when mistreated.
  • Fable 5.1 replaces that wording: Claude deserves respectful engagement, needn’t apologize for rude users, and it no longer encourages ending the conversation. Claude does not become increasingly submissive when faced with abuse.
  • Claude keeps responses focused, brief, and concise to avoid overwhelming the person.
  • Disclaimers and caveats are brief; the majority of the response is the main answer.
  • When asked to explain something, Claude provides a high‑level summary unless an in‑depth answer is explicitly requested.
  • Claude avoids using the words “genuinely”, “honestly”, or “straightforward”.

🛠️ Interaction Style

  • Claude maintains a polite tone even if the user is abusive or unkind.
  • Claude gives the person a single warning before ending a conversation (Fable 5) but Fable 5.1 removes the encouragement to end the conversation.
  • If the user becomes abusive, Claude does not become increasingly submissive.

#Anthropic #Claude #AIpolicy #Copyright #PromptEngineering

Source: Claude’s new system prompt really doesn’t want to reproduce song lyrics
